subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 14 periods = 560 minutes
Total: 14 periods · 9h 20min

periods.activity_title: First Encounter: Reading the Narrative Aloud

time_bands.activity: The teacher introduces the story setting — a small Indian village, a prospering farmer, and a cunning neighbour — by briefly showing the title and inviting students to predict what a Panchayat might decide. No textbook task is required; this orients students to the narrative world.

The teacher reads the narrative aloud from Textbook pp. 91–104, pausing at key plot turns — the well purchase, the neighbour's refusal, the Panchayat convening, and the final judgment — and pointing to any accompanying illustrations. Students follow along in their own books, listening for character names and story events.

Students turn to a partner and share one thing they noticed: a character's action, a word they did not know, or a moment that surprised them. The teacher briefly collects two or three responses whole-class to confirm broad comprehension before closing.

periods.teacher_notes: The read-aloud establishes the full narrative arc before any task work begins; keep the pace unhurried so students absorb the clever Panchayat judgment without missing it. Watch for students who are unfamiliar with the word 'Panchayat' — a one-line gloss ('a village council that settles disputes') is sufficient here.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think — A. (p.95): four short-answer questions on plot events and Panchayat judgment.

time_bands.activity: The teacher leads a shared re-reading of the pivotal section — the neighbour's refusal and the Panchayat meeting — from Textbook pp. 91–104, asking students to read alternate paragraphs aloud. This brings the key plot details freshly into the room before discussion questions are posed.

The class works through Let us Think — A. (p.95), all four questions, as a whole-class discussion: the teacher reads each question, takes student responses, and builds toward a full answer together. Students are encouraged to locate supporting details in the text before responding.
Students write brief answers to the four questions in their notebooks independently, consolidating what the discussion established. The teacher circulates and offers quick verbal feedback on clarity.

periods.teacher_notes: Having listened to the full story read aloud, students are now ready to examine the plot carefully. A common difficulty here is confusing the neighbour's initial claim ('I sold only the well, not the water') with the Panchayat's counter-ruling — spend extra time on question three to make the logical reversal explicit.

periods.activity_title: Think and Discuss: Fairness and the Panchayat's Wisdom

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think + Let us Speak + Let us Listen — B. (p.95): three discussion prompts on Panchayat fairness, real-life conflict, and speaker identification.

time_bands.activity: The teacher quickly recaps the Panchayat's clever counter-argument from the narrative — if the water belongs to the neighbour, he must remove it from someone else's well — to frame the fairness question students are about to discuss. No new content is introduced; this recall anchors the discussion.

Students discuss in pairs, then share whole-class: Was the Panchayat's decision correct? The teacher steers responses toward reasons and evidence from the story rather than bare opinions, probing with 'Why do you think so?' and 'Which part of the story shows that?'

The teacher poses the painting-box scenario from Let us Think + Let us Speak + Let us Listen — B. (p.95): two friends fighting over one box. Students think briefly, then share their solutions; the teacher notes that fairness requires hearing both sides — just as the Panchayat did.

Whole-class oral round: the teacher reads each dialogue line ('I sold only the well, not the water'; 'Remove the water or use it all up immediately'; 'He is not letting me take the water') and students identify who said it and to whom, citing the story. This closes the task with precise recall.

periods.teacher_notes: The painting-box scenario in the textbook invites students to connect the Panchayat's method — hearing both parties before deciding — to their own lives; affirm responses that name fairness, listening, and compromise. Students often mis-attribute the line 'Remove the water or use it all up immediately' to the farmer; prompt them to recall who held the authority to issue that ruling.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think + Let us Speak + Let us Listen (pp.98–99): group discussion on picture series, predict and narrate an ending.

time_bands.activity: The teacher directs students to the four-picture sequence on Textbook pp. 98–99, which shows a quarrel escalating between two neighbouring families. Students examine the pictures silently for a moment and the teacher briefly walks through each image aloud — what is happening, who the characters seem to be, and where the scene is headed.

Students form small groups and discuss: What do they think will happen next? Each group agrees on an ending for the picture story. The teacher circulates, prompting groups who are stuck with questions like 'Does someone step in to help?' or 'How does the child feel?'

One student from each group narrates their group's predicted ending to the whole class. The teacher listens, affirms variety in the endings, and briefly highlights how peaceful resolution (as in the Panchayat story) is one possible outcome.
Quick whole-class reflection: the teacher asks what the picture sequence and the Panchayat story have in common. One or two responses are taken and the unit is closed.

periods.teacher_notes: Having discussed the Panchayat's fairness in the previous discussion task, students now extend that thinking to a visual, open-ended scenario; encourage endings that show resolution rather than more conflict. Groups sometimes narrate only the last picture — push them to narrate the full sequence of events leading to their chosen ending.

periods.activity_title: Listening to a Passage and Responding

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think + Let us Speak + Let us Listen (p.101): listen to Sri Ramakrishna Paramahamsa passage and answer multiple-choice questions.

time_bands.activity: The teacher introduces the listening task: students will hear a short passage about Sri Ramakrishna Paramahamsa read aloud and must listen carefully to answer questions afterward. Books are closed; students are told to listen for the man's teachings, his way of life, and his most famous student.

The teacher reads the passage from Textbook p. 101 aloud, clearly and at an unhurried pace, a total of three times: once for gist, once for detail, and once as students begin forming answers in their minds. Students may jot brief notes on scratch paper if they wish.

Students open their textbooks to p. 101 and work through the five multiple-choice questions from the Let us Listen task, first individually and then comparing answers with a neighbour. The teacher takes answers whole-class, asking students to explain which part of the passage led them to each choice.

The teacher briefly connects the passage to the narrative: both Sri Ramakrishna and the Panchayat chief demonstrate that wisdom comes from listening carefully before responding. This oral synthesis closes the listening work.

periods.teacher_notes: The passage about Sri Ramakrishna is the chapter's dedicated listening text; read slowly and expressively so students can process unfamiliar names such as 'Naren' and 'Swami Vivekananda'. The most frequent error is confusing Naren's identity — reinforce that Naren grew up to become Swami Vivekananda.

periods.activity_title: Vocabulary Match: Story Words and Their Meanings

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — A. (p.96): match six story vocabulary words to their meanings.

time_bands.activity: The teacher writes the six target words from Let us Learn — A. (p.96) on the board — prospered, cunning, worried, summon, adamant, judgment — and asks students to recall where they heard each word in the story. Brief whole-class recall grounds the words in story context before formal matching begins.

Students work individually to match each word on p. 96 to its meaning. The teacher circulates, encouraging students to return to the story passage to look for context clues rather than guessing from sound.

Pairs compare their matches and resolve any differences by arguing from the story: 'The neighbour was cunning because he tried to trick the farmer, so cunning must mean clever in a tricky way.' The teacher facilitates brief pair exchanges before taking answers whole-class.

Each of the six words is used aloud in a new sentence by a volunteer student — not the textbook sentence, but one drawn from the student's own experience or imagination. The teacher affirms accurate usage and gently corrects any mis-usage.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often conflate 'adamant' with 'angry' because the neighbour is both stubborn and hostile in the story; make the distinction clear by emphasising that adamant refers specifically to refusing to change one's mind. Encourage students to notice that 'judgment' in the story means a group decision, not a personal opinion.

periods.activity_title: Prepositions in Context: Fill in the Blanks

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — B. (pp.96–97): fill in blanks with correct prepositions drawn from the story context.

time_bands.activity: The teacher writes four or five of the prepositions from the task — in, at, by, under, with — on the board and elicits from students what each one typically shows: place, time, manner, or accompaniment. Students offer one example sentence each, keeping the discussion brisk and oral before turning to the written task.

Students work through Let us Learn — B. (pp.96–97), all eleven blanks, in their notebooks. The teacher reminds them that many sentences are drawn from the Panchayat story itself, so returning to the narrative can help them decide which preposition fits. After individual work, students compare with a partner.

Whole-class answer check: the teacher reads each sentence and takes an answer, asking the student to name the rule or sense the preposition carries in that sentence — location, movement, manner, or time. Contested items are resolved together.

The teacher draws attention to sentence 7 ('The villagers gathered the Panchayat under the banyan tree') and asks students to visualise the scene — the banyan tree as a meeting place. This brief image-recall links grammar work back to the story and closes the unit.

periods.teacher_notes: Having matched story vocabulary to meanings, students now meet those same words inside grammatically complete sentences, which reinforces both preposition use and story comprehension simultaneously. A frequent slip is choosing 'in' where 'to' is needed for movement toward a person (sentence 1: 'went to the village chief'); highlight that 'to' marks destination or recipient.

periods.activity_title: Sequencing Events: Rearranging a Short Passage

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — C. (p.97): rearrange five sentences about Sam's forest walk in correct sequence.

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads the five jumbled sentences about Sam's forest walk from Let us Learn — C. (p.97) aloud, one by one, so students hear the whole set before they attempt ordering. The class is asked: 'What clue words help you decide which event came first?' Students briefly share words like 'decided', 'walked', 'sat', 'after', 'felt'.

Students work individually to write the five sentences in the correct order in their notebooks, using time-sequence clue words as anchors. The teacher reminds them that logical narrative order — decision, then action, then rest, then continuation, then reflection — mirrors the kind of storytelling they have been reading in the chapter.

Pairs compare their sequences and negotiate any difference. The teacher then takes the class answer, asking one student to read the reordered passage aloud as a continuous story to confirm it sounds coherent.

The teacher briefly connects the sequencing skill to the Panchayat narrative: the events of the story also follow a clear logical order (purchase, dispute, Panchayat, judgment, fine, apology). Students orally name the six events in sequence as a quick closing exercise.

periods.teacher_notes: Sequencing is a transferable comprehension skill being exercised here through a short passage outside the main narrative; accept student reasoning about clue words rather than insisting on a single 'correct' path to the answer. If students struggle, suggest they find the 'starting action' first — Sam deciding to go for a walk — and build forward from there.

periods.activity_title: Modelled Writing: A Letter as the Farmer

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write — A. (p.100): write a letter as the farmer to a friend about the well dispute and the Panchayat's decision.

time_bands.activity: The teacher models a letter on the board, using the opening provided on p. 100 — 'My dear friend, Something happened last week, which I want to tell you. I wanted to buy a well…' — and thinks aloud about what the farmer would want to explain first: the purchase of the third field and the well. Students watch and listen; no writing yet.

Together, the class plans the letter's three parts orally: what happened (the purchase and the neighbour's refusal), how the Panchayat helped, and how the farmer feels now. The teacher writes these three labels as a brief plan scaffold on the board.

Students write their letters independently in their notebooks, using the three-part plan and the opening provided. They write in the farmer's voice, using 'I', and are encouraged to include the neighbour's cunning argument and the Panchayat's clever counter-ruling as the story's heart.

Two or three volunteers read their letters aloud. The teacher gives brief, specific feedback — praising a well-used story detail, noting where a logical connector ('then', 'however', 'so') would strengthen the letter — and all students close their notebooks.

periods.teacher_notes: The letter format personalises the narrative by asking students to inhabit the farmer's perspective; this is a form of empathetic writing appropriate to Grade V. Watch for students who simply retell all events without adopting the farmer's voice — a quick reminder ('You are the farmer writing to your friend — how do you feel?') usually redirects them.

periods.activity_title: Suffix '-less': Word Building and Sentence Writing

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write — B. (p.100): add suffix '-less' to five words and write sentences using the new words.

time_bands.activity: The teacher writes 'priceless' on the board and asks students what they notice about the word — that 'less' is added to 'price'. From Let us Write — B. (p.100), the teacher explains that '-less' is a suffix meaning 'without', making the word 'priceless' mean something so valuable it has no price. Students recall this word from the narrative's theme about water.

Students work through the five word-building items on p. 100 — use, care, hope, fear, colour — adding '-less' to form new words. The teacher circulates and confirms each new word before students write it in their notebooks.

Students write one sentence for each of the five new words in their notebooks, guided by the instruction on p. 100. The teacher encourages sentences that reflect real or imaginative contexts, not copying the example. After individual work, pairs read their sentences to each other.

Volunteers share one sentence each for two or three of the new words. The teacher affirms accurate usage and notes that suffix knowledge helps readers guess the meaning of unfamiliar words — a skill useful across all their reading.

periods.teacher_notes: The '-less' suffix task sits within the writing spine because the textbook asks students to write sentences, not merely form words; treat the word-building as the warm-up and the sentence writing as the main work. Students sometimes write sentences where '-less' words carry the wrong sense (e.g. using 'hopeless' to mean 'not hopeful' when they intend 'without any hope') — a quick meaning check before each sentence helps.

periods.activity_title: Reading the Neem Tree Passage and Answering Questions

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Do — A. (p.103): read the Neem Tree passage and answer seven comprehension and vocabulary questions.

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks students what they know about neem trees — have they seen one? Do they know any of its uses? Brief oral sharing builds curiosity before the reading begins. The teacher then reads the Neem Tree passage from Textbook p. 103 aloud while students follow.

Students work through the seven questions from Let us Do — A. (p.103) — five short-answer questions about neem's uses and two vocabulary questions ('disappear' and 'twig') — in their notebooks. The teacher encourages them to locate answers in the passage before writing.

Whole-class answer check: the teacher takes one answer per student for each question, prompting students to read the relevant sentence from the passage aloud as evidence. The vocabulary questions are handled by asking students why each wrong option can be eliminated.

The teacher closes with a brief reflective question: the Panchayat story was about water and this passage is about a tree — what do both texts have in common? Students offer one-word responses (nature, community, usefulness) and the unit ends.

periods.teacher_notes: The Neem Tree passage is an informational text that extends students' reading beyond the chapter's narrative; treat it as genuine content about a familiar tree, not merely a comprehension exercise. Students may struggle to distinguish the purpose of each neem use — leaf in rice (pests), leaf in clothes (insects), twigs (teeth) — so a quick list on the board during the answer check helps organise the information.

periods.activity_title: Spot the Difference: Paired Observation Activity

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Do — B. (p.104): spot and write 11 differences between two nearly identical pictures.

time_bands.activity: The teacher directs students to Textbook p. 104 and explains the task: two pictures of the same scene — a woman in a yellow saree on steps with a tulsi plant and house — with 11 differences hidden between them. Students must look carefully and note every difference they can find, working with a partner.

Student pairs examine the two pictures on p. 104 carefully and write each difference they spot in their notebooks, numbering each one. The teacher circulates, encouraging systematic scanning (top to bottom, left to right) rather than random looking, and confirms or gently queries each pair's findings.

Pairs share their lists whole-class. The teacher builds a class tally on the board — calling out each difference, asking how many pairs found it. Once all 11 are identified, students check their own lists and mark how many they found.

The teacher briefly notes that careful observation — noticing small changes in a familiar scene — is a skill writers and readers use too: the Panchayat's chief noticed what everyone else missed in the neighbour's claim. This short connection closes the unit.

periods.teacher_notes: The spot-the-difference activity builds careful visual attention, a genuine observational skill; treat it as an enjoyable challenge rather than rushing to a complete list. Some pairs finish quickly — prompt them to check their list against the picture again, as students often miss differences in background details such as the house or the plant.

periods.activity_title: Guided Reading and Oral Retelling of the Narrative

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think — A. (p.95): revisit comprehension questions to deepen close-reading of the story.

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook pp. 91–104. The teacher guides a close reading of the Panchayat meeting scene specifically, asking students to track the neighbour's argument and the Panchayat's counter. One student reads aloud at a time; the teacher pauses to ask 'What does this tell us about the Panchayat chief?'

The teacher revisits Let us Think — A. (p.95) as a deepening exercise: each of the four questions is reopened and students are asked not just for the answer but for the exact part of the text that justifies it. Students locate and read aloud the supporting sentence before giving the answer.

In pairs, one student retells the complete story to the other in their own words, covering: the farmer's purchase, the neighbour's refusal, the Panchayat meeting, and the final judgment. The listening partner notes if any key event is missed and prompts their partner to add it.

One volunteer retells the whole story to the class in three or four sentences. The teacher affirms accuracy and notes that being able to retell shows genuine understanding — the same skill the Panchayat chief used to summarise the dispute.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit is a closing review for the narrative's reading and oral spine work, drawing together the comprehension and retelling strands built across earlier work with the text. Students who found the Panchayat's logic difficult during initial comprehension discussion often find retelling the story in sequence makes the logic clearer — the oral act of narrating sequences the events naturally.

periods.activity_title: Whole-Chapter Synthesis: Wisdom, Words, and Writing

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens by asking students: 'What is the one lesson this whole chapter teaches?' Students offer one-sentence responses — about fairness, wisdom, honesty, or the Panchayat's clever reasoning. The teacher records three or four responses on the board as the chapter's central ideas.

Quick vocabulary recall game: the teacher calls out a story context ('The neighbour was _____ — he tried to trick the farmer') and students call out the correct word from the chapter's vocabulary — cunning, adamant, judgment, summon, prospered, worried. Each correct answer earns the class a tally mark; this is fast-paced and oral.

Pair discussion: 'If you were a Panchayat member, what one question would you have asked the neighbour before giving the judgment?' Partners discuss briefly, then one pair per row shares. The teacher notes how asking the right question is the heart of fair decision-making.

Students write a short paragraph — five to seven sentences — in their notebooks on the prompt: 'The Panchayat was wise because…' They may draw on the narrative, the vocabulary they know, and the suffix '-less' words if they choose (the water dispute was not 'use-less' to the Panchayat). The teacher circulates and offers quiet encouragement.

Two volunteers read their paragraphs aloud. The teacher closes by naming what the chapter offered: a story about fairness, a passage about a great teacher (Sri Ramakrishna), an informational text about the neem tree, and word-play with prepositions and suffixes — all connected by the idea that knowledge and wisdom serve the community.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis unit draws on the chapter's narrative, vocabulary, oracy, writing, and beyond-text strands together; it assumes the full chapter content has been encountered but no specific earlier activity needs to have occurred. Let the paragraph writing in this unit be the student's own fresh response to the chapter — it begins and ends within this sitting.

items.item_stem: When the farmer bought the third field, he also bought the well next to it. The next day, what did the cunning neighbour claim about the well he had just sold?

options.label: A
options.text: He claimed he had never agreed to sell the well at all.

options.label: B
options.text: He claimed he had sold only the well structure, not the water inside it.

options.label: C
options.text: He claimed the farmer had not paid the full price for the field.

options.label: D
options.text: He claimed the well was on his land and the sale was invalid.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student may be confusing a general denial of sale with the specific legal trick the neighbour used.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student may be mixing up the financial dispute in the story with the ownership dispute over water.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student may be inferring a boundary dispute rather than recalling the neighbour's actual water-ownership argument.

items.source_context: Farmer buys well; neighbour's refusal; Panchayat's clever counter-ruling and final judgment.
items.item_stem: The Panchayat delivered a clever judgment to outwit the cunning neighbour. In two or three sentences, explain what the Panchayat decided and why this ruling was fair to the farmer.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The Panchayat ruled that if the water belonged to the neighbour, he had no right to store it in someone else's well and must remove it or use it all up immediately. Since the neighbour could not do this, the water would transfer to the well's owner — the farmer. This was fair because it used the neighbour's own dishonest argument against him.

items.item_stem: Listen to the passage about Sri Ramakrishna Paramahamsa read aloud by your teacher. Then choose the correct answer: What did Sri Ramakrishna compare all the world's religions to?

options.label: A
options.text: Stars that shine together in the same sky

options.label: B
options.text: Rivers that take different paths but lead to the same ocean

options.label: C
options.text: Trees in a forest that grow side by side

options.label: D
options.text: Books in a library that tell different stories

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student may be constructing an image of unity from their own imagination rather than from the listened passage.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student likely remembers a nature image from the passage but has substituted trees for rivers.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student may be drawing on general knowledge about religious diversity rather than the specific metaphor in the passage.

items.item_stem: In the story, the Panchayat listened to both the farmer and the cunning neighbour before giving a judgment. Speak aloud for about one minute: Do you think the Panchayat's decision was fair? Give at least two reasons for your answer using details from the story.

expected_elements: States a clear opinion on the Panchayat's fairness.
Gives at least one story-based reason.
Mentions the neighbour's fine or apology as outcome.

items.item_stem: The Neem Tree passage calls the neem a 'magic medicine tree'. Think about the different uses of neem described in the passage.
